# Workload identity for the Reducto API

Call Reducto with short-lived tokens from your existing identity provider instead of a long-lived API key.

![Workload identity for the Reducto API](https://cdn.reducto.ai/blogs/workload-identity/hero-exchange.png)

Our customers send us loan files, medical records, contracts and tax returns, so we spend a lot of our engineering time on security. We don't use long-lived API keys to call AI models inside Reducto, and now our customers don't need one to call us either, with Workload Identity.

Here's why API keys became a target, what replaces them, and how to use it with Reducto.

## A rise in distillation attacks

In February Anthropic [wrote](https://www.anthropic.com/news/detecting-and-preventing-distillation-attacks) about three AI labs that tried to distill Claude, meaning they trained their own models on its outputs. They ran over 16 million exchanges through about 24,000 fraudulent accounts, a lot of it through proxy services that resell access to frontier models.

Fake accounts get banned, so the next step was obvious: steal real keys from companies that already have high rate limits. October was rough for developer platforms.

- [OpenCode](https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/19/hackers-hit-ai-coding-tool-opencode-running-up-charges-on-users-ai-accounts/), the open source coding agent, said attackers got into an older system and reached the OpenAI, Anthropic and Google keys that 1.4% of its Console users had stored there. OpenCode tied the breach to "a large-scale distillation attack."
- Days later [Railway](https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/22/developer-platform-railway-urges-all-users-to-revoke-secret-keys-after-cyberattack/) said an attacker may have decrypted some customers' environment variables, and told every user to rotate their keys.

The pattern is clear. A high-limit OpenAI or Anthropic key used to be a billing problem if it leaked, and now people actively hunt for it. Startups are an easy place to find them because their keys have high limits and are spread across laptops, CI and a dozen services.

The simplest defense is not to hold keys at all.

## What's wrong with API keys

An API key is like a password for a machine. It never expires unless someone remembers to rotate it, so a key pasted into a CI secret in 2023 probably still works. It's a bearer secret, which means whoever has it is you, and it can't tell which machine is using it. And it gets copied into env files, CI settings, Slack messages and logs, each of which is one more place it can leak from.

Rotating keys helps, but you're still storing a secret, just a newer one.

API key

rd_live_8f2c… valid until someone deletes it

Federated token

day 1month 6year 2

## OIDC and workload identity

Almost always, your code already runs somewhere that knows who it is. A GitHub Actions job knows its repo and branch, and a Kubernetes pod knows its service account. AWS roles, Azure managed identities and Google service accounts know who they are too.

These platforms can prove it with an **OIDC token**, a short JSON Web Token that the platform signs. It says who the workload is (`sub`), who issued the token (`iss`), who it's for (`aud`) and when it expires (`exp`), usually within an hour. Anyone can check the signature against the issuer's public keys.

**Workload identity federation** builds on this. The workload hands its platform token to the service it wants to call. The service checks the signature and the claims, matches them against rules you set, and gives back its own short-lived token. Nobody stores a long-lived secret.

Workload

GitHub Actions job
`acme/payments@main`

Platform issuer

`token.actions.githubusercontent.com`

Reducto

`POST /oauth/token`
check signature, claims, mapping

Reducto API

`/parse` `/extract`

`id_token` · 5 min

`id_token` → exchange

`rdat_…` · ≤ 1 h

`Bearer rdat_…`

1 Ask the platform who I am2 Trade that for a Reducto token3 Reducto checks the rules4 Call the API. No key stored.

Here is a trimmed token from a GitHub Actions job:

```
json{
  "iss": "https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com",
  "aud": "https://platform.reducto.ai",
  "sub": "repo:acme/payments:ref:refs/heads/main",
  "repository": "acme/payments",
  "ref": "refs/heads/main",
  "exp": 1793322545
}
```

If your rule says `sub` must start with `repo:acme/payments:` and `ref` must be `refs/heads/main`, only the main branch of that repo can get a token. Forks, feature branches and anyone holding a copied config file get nothing.

**X.509** does the same thing for workloads that have certificates instead of tokens. A lot of companies run their own certificate authority, a service mesh or SPIFFE, and those workloads already have a client certificate and a private key that stays on the machine. The workload proves who it is during the TLS handshake (mutual TLS), and we bind the token we issue to that certificate. A stolen token is useless without the private key.

## How we use it at Reducto

Due to the nature of the sensitive data we process, security has always been a critical part of our operations at Reducto. A few things we support:

- **Hybrid VPC.** Your documents and results stay in your own bucket (S3, Azure Blob, Google Cloud Storage or Box) while we run the GPUs. On AWS we reach your bucket through a cross-account role with an external ID, and on Azure through a managed identity in your tenant, so we never store a storage secret.
- **Least privilege.** Each service, GPU worker and CI job gets its own identity with only the permissions it needs. Our CI jobs read secrets through OIDC instead of storing them in GitHub.
- **The basics, audited.** SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA with a BAA, AES-256 at rest, TLS 1.2+ in transit.

We use the same federation for our own AI credentials. Our API pods, GPU workers, agent service and CI jobs get short-lived tokens for Anthropic, OpenAI and OpenRouter from their own platform identity.

API pods

Anthropic · OpenAI · OpenRouter

OIDC→short-lived token

GPU workers (Modal)

OpenAI · Anthropic

OIDC→short-lived token

Agent service

OpenAI · OpenRouter

OIDC→short-lived token

CI (GitHub Actions)

Anthropic · OpenAI · Doppler

OIDC→short-lived token

Each service has to get a few things right: refresh the token before it expires, run only one exchange at a time, and fail cleanly instead of falling back to a key. A leaked config file, laptop or CI log from Reducto has nothing in it that can call a model.

## Doing the same for our customers

Our customers have security teams that are trying to get rid of long-lived keys too, and a Reducto API key sitting in their CI secrets is one more item on that list. We'd like to be the vendor they can cross off quickly.

So Reducto now supports workload identity federation directly:

- **Your existing identity provider.** GitHub Actions, Kubernetes, AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Oracle Cloud, SPIFFE, or any issuer that signs standard JWTs.
- **Rules in Studio.** Add an identity provider, then add mappings on the token's claims. You can paste a real token to test your rules before you ship.
- **Short-lived tokens.** Reducto returns an access token that lasts an hour or less. If you disable a mapping, its tokens stop working within 60 seconds.
- **X.509 and mTLS.** Upload your CA as a trust anchor. A token issued from a certificate only works alongside that certificate.

![Workload identity settings in Reducto Studio](https://cdn.reducto.ai/blogs/workload-identity/fig-studio.webp)

The SDKs do most of the work. The Python and Node SDKs exchange, cache and refresh tokens for you, and they ship token providers for GitHub Actions, Kubernetes (EKS, GKE, AKS or self-managed), AWS, Azure managed identity and Google Cloud. Picking one is usually a single line:

```
pythonfrom reducto import Reducto
from reducto.auth import github_actions_token_provider

client = Reducto(
    workload_identity={
        "identity_provider_id": "wip_...",
        "provider": github_actions_token_provider("https://platform.reducto.ai"),
    }
)
```

If your tokens come from somewhere else, you write a small provider with a `get_token` function and the SDK calls it whenever it needs a fresh token. Our Oracle Cloud guide has an example.

Workload identity federation is available to every Reducto organization today. Once it's set up, you can delete your Reducto API key.
